{{Short description|Type of partial category}}

[[File:Category_SVG.svg|thumbnail|For comparison, this diagram shows a typical [[Morphism|arrow]] composition in an ordinary category. (Without arrow composition, it is simply a directed graph.) The arrows <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> in the diagram are consecutive; they connect in <math>B = \text{cod} (f) = \text{dom} (g).</math> In an ordinary category, the composition of any pair of consecutive arrows exists, whereas in a multiplicative graph, a pair of consecutive arrows is not necessarily composable.<ref>{{harvnb|Cury|2004}}</ref>]]

In [[mathematics]], a '''multiplicative graph''' (in French: '''{{lang|fr|graphe multiplicatif}}''' or '''neocategory'''{{R|BastianiEhresmann1972}} in some English-language papers) is an [[algebraic structure]] in [[category theory]]. It is a generalization of an [[Category (mathematics)|ordinary category]] in the sense that neither the [[Category (mathematics)#Definition|associativity]] of arrow composition nor the [[Binary operation|composibility]] of a pair of connected arrows are assumed. While an ordinary category is a notion combining a [[directed graph]] and a [[Monoid|monoidal structure]], a multiplicative graph is a [[partial groupoid|partial magma-like structure]]. Namely, it is a structure in [[#Definition|one‑to‑one correspondence with the vertices of a directed graph]], and each object has [[Category (mathematics)#Definition|left and right identity morphisms]], but composability is partial, and, moreover, associativity is not required.<ref name="BastianiEhresmann1972">{{harvnb|Bastiani|Ehresmann|1972|loc=§1. Neocategories and neofunctors.}}</ref>

Arrow composition in an ordinary category satisfies the following property: if arrows <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> connect in the sense that <math>\text{dom} (g) = \text{cod} (f),</math> their composition <math>g \circ f</math> is defined, and, moreover, <math>\text{dom} (g \circ f) = \text{dom} (f)</math> and <math>\text{cod} (g \circ f) = \text{cod} (g).</math> In a multiplicative graph, however, condition <math>\text{dom} (g) = \text{cod} (f)</math> does not guarantee the existence of <math>g \circ f</math> within that structure without further assumptions – but ''if'' this composition exists, it also satisfies <math>\text{dom} (g \circ f) = \text{dom} (f)</math> and <math>\text{cod} (g \circ f) = \text{cod} (g).</math><ref>{{harvnb|Coppey|1980|loc=Introduction.}}</ref> When drawing a diagram for a multiplicative graph, it is almost always necessary to explicitly draw all existing arrows that play a role in the argument. For example, as shown in Coppey (1980), square diagrams in a multiplicative graph can take one of five types depending on which potential compositions in the diagram are actually defined.<ref>{{harvnb|Coppey|1980|loc=2. Produits tensoriels (unitaires) et fermetures.}}</ref>

This notion first appears in Ehresmann's book ''Catégories et structures''.<ref>{{harvnb|Ehresmann|1965|loc=ch. I, Dèfinition 8.}}</ref> The French school bases its definition of [[Sketch (mathematics)|sketch]] on the notion of a multiplicative graph,{{R|Wells2009}} because this definition required a category-like structure that avoided redundant axioms as much as possible.<ref>{{harvnb|Cury|2004|loc=INTRODUCTION}}</ref> This structure is the multiplicative graph, and this is a type of relaxed notion of category, such as a [[semicategory]].{{R|MateusSernadasSernadas1999}}

Cury studied [[enriched category|enriched]] multiplicative graph.<ref>{{harvnb|Cury|1979}}</ref> As a more general notion, there is the compositional graph, and multiplicative graphs can be seen as [[two-sided identity|strongly identitive]] compositional graphs.<ref name=MateusSernadasSernadas1999>{{harvnb|Mateus|Sernadas|Sernadas|1999}}</ref>

==Definition==
{{Group-like structures}}
A multiplicative graph <math>\Sigma</math> is couple formed by a set denoted by <math>\underline{\Sigma}</math>, and a [[Partial operation|partial law]] of composition <math>\kappa</math> on <math>\underline{\Sigma}</math> satisfying the following axioms:{{R|BastianiEhresmann1972}}<ref>{{harvnb|Ehresmann|1965|loc=ch. I, §.B) Graphes multiplicatifs et catègories. For the definition of "classe multiplicative", see ch. I, § A) Classes multiplicatives.}}</ref>

# <math>\kappa</math> is a mapping from a subset of <math>\underline{\Sigma} \times \underline{\Sigma}</math> (denoted by <math>\Sigma * \Sigma</math> and called the set of composable couples) into <math>\underline{\Sigma}</math>; instead of <math>\kappa(y, x)</math>, we write <math>y \circ x</math> and we call <math>y \circ x</math> the composite of <math>(y, x)</math>.
# There exists a [[Quiver (mathematics)#Reflexive quiver|reflexive graph]]<ref name=Wells2009>{{harvnb|Wells|2009|loc=11.3 Compositive graphs}}</ref> <math>(\underline{\Sigma}, \beta, \alpha)</math> (i.e. <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are [[Section (category theory)|retractions]] from <math>\underline{\Sigma}</math> onto a subset of <math>\underline{\Sigma}</math>, denoted by <math>\Sigma_0</math>), such that:

:(existence of units<ref>{{harvnb|Ehresmann|1965|loc=ch. I, Dèfinition 8. (G<sub>1</sub>)}}</ref><ref name="Coppey1980">{{harvnb|Coppey|1980|loc=1. Graphes multiplicatifs, foncteurs, transformations naturelles.}}</ref> {{bracket|existence of composition for [[Loop (graph theory)|loops]]}}):  For each element <math>x</math> of <math>\underline{\Sigma}</math>, the composites <math>x \circ \alpha (x)</math> and <math>\beta (x) \circ x</math> are defined, and we have
::<math>x \circ \alpha(x) = x = \beta (x) \circ x.</math>
::Here, <math>\alpha(x)</math> is the [[right identity]] of <math>x</math> and is called the source of <math>x</math>, while <math>\beta (x)</math> is the [[left identity]] of <math>x</math> and is called the target of <math>x</math>;

:(coherence of dom/cod{{R|Coppey1980}}<ref>{{harvnb|Ehresmann|1965|loc=ch. I, Dèfinition 8. (G<sub>2</sub>)}}</ref>): If the composite <math>y \circ x</math> is defined, then:
::<math>\alpha(y \circ x) = \alpha (x), \ \beta(y \circ x) = \beta (y), \ \text{and} \  \alpha (y) = \beta (x).</math>

From the condition 2, the reflexive graph <math>(\Sigma, \beta, \alpha)</math> is uniquely defined.

==Inverse morphisms are not unique==
Let <math>C^*</math> be a multiplicative graph, if one has a <math>(f, f') \in C^{*} * C^{*}
</math> and <math>f \circ f' = \beta(f)</math> (resp. <math>(f', f) \in C^{*} * C^{*}</math> and <math>f' \circ f = \alpha(f)</math>), then we say that <math>f \in C</math> admit a right (resp. left) inverse of a morphism <math>f'</math> in <math>C^*</math>. If there exists an <math>f' \in C</math>, we say that <math>f</math> in <math>C^*</math> is invertible such that <math>f'</math> is the right and left inverse of <math>f</math> in <math>C^*</math>, then we called <math>f'</math> an inverse of <math>f</math> in <math>C^*</math>. If <math>C^*</math> is a multiplicative graph and if <math>f \in C</math> admit f' for right (resp. left) inverse in <math>C^*</math>, one has:

<math>\alpha(f') = \beta(f)</math> and <math>\beta(f') = \alpha(f)</math>

While inverse morphisms in a ordinary category are unique, a morphisme of multiplicative graph <math>C^*</math> can have several inverse morphisms.<ref>{{harvnb|Ehresmann|1965|loc=C) Eléments inversibles et groupoïdes.}}</ref> The law of composition  are shown in the table below:

[[File:Inverse morphisms in a multiplicative graph.svg|thumb]]
{| class="wikitable"
|-
| ||f||f'||f<nowiki>''</nowiki>||e||e'
|-
|f|| ||e'||e'||f|| 
|-
|f'||e|| || || ||f'
|-
|f<nowiki>''</nowiki>||e|| || || ||f<nowiki>''</nowiki>
|-
|e|| ||f'||f<nowiki>''</nowiki>||e||
|-
|e'||f|| || || ||e'
|}

==Example==
*An ordinary category is a multiplicative graph if it satisfies the following two axioms:{{R|BastianiEhresmann1972}}{{R|Coppey1980}}<ref>{{harvnb|Ehresmann|1965|loc=ch. I, Dèfinition 11.}}</ref>
:(composibility):all the couples <math>(y, x)</math> where <math>\alpha (y) = \beta (x)</math> are composable (so that <math>\Sigma * \Sigma</math> is the [[Pullback (category theory)|pullback]] of <math>(\alpha, \beta)</math>);
:(strong associativity):the law of composition being furthermore associative.
*For the two axioms above, a notion got by adding only the associativity axiom (that is, associativity is not strong) to a multiplicative graph, that is, a notion that an ordinary category without the composibility axiom, this is called a precategory.{{R|Coppey1980}} But, this is not standard terminology, a precategory is usually synonymous with a [[semigroupoid]] and does not require each object to have an identity morphism.
